answers.answer: The client contacts the service entry point, the reverse proxy forwards to a selected application server, that server performs the application work and database access, and the response returns through the balancer to the client. Choose L7 for /search and /purchase routing because it understands HTTP paths. It needs readable HTTP contents; an HTTPS proxy normally terminates client TLS to inspect requests, with backend encryption configured separately. L4 normally selects a backend per TCP connection using network information. Many HTTP requests can reuse that connection and remain on its selected backend without fresh selection. A single adequate server can suffice without a balancer when distribution or redundant serving is unnecessary.

evidence.quote: In this reverse-proxy example, the client contacts one service entry point. The balancer forwards the request to a selected backend. That server reads the note from the database and returns a response through the balancer to the client.

Understands HTTP requests. It can route /notes and /exports to different backend groups, or select a backend for each request. Rules that keep a user on one backend can override independent selection.

Path routing requires readable HTTP contents. TLS encrypts the connection; an HTTPS proxy normally ends, or terminates, that TLS connection to inspect requests. Encryption to the backend is a separate configuration choice.
Routes at the transport level. For TCP traffic, it typically chooses a backend for a connection using network information, not HTTP paths.
Many note requests can reuse that connection. They can all reach the same backend; adding requests on that connection does not force new selections.
One adequate server may be enough if the service does not need traffic distribution or redundant serving. A balancer is not automatically useful in front of it.

answers.answer: Round robin takes turns among eligible servers and is simple for similar servers and work, but counts a cheap lookup and a long request equally. Least connections prefers fewer active connections and may help with differing durations, but a connection count can hide very different amounts of work. Weights control traffic share: twice the measured capacity suggests twice the initial weight, but the configured ratio is neither live capacity measurement nor a performance guarantee. Check latency and resource use. More application servers cannot remove the shared saturated database bottleneck, so they alone may not increase throughput. Availability after a machine fails requires a reachable alternate entry path or available managed entry with tested failover, and enough spare capacity on surviving backends for the load. Excess work must be limited or visibly rejected when survivors lack capacity.

evidence.quote: Takes turns across eligible backends. It is a simple starting point for similar servers and similar work; a quick note read and a slow export still each count as one request.
Prefers the backend with fewer active connections. This can help when connection durations vary, but one connection may carry far more work than another.
Bias the share of traffic. A server with twice the measured capacity might start with twice the weight. Configured weights are not a live measurement or a performance guarantee.
For long, uneven work, consider least connections; for unequal server capacity, consider weights. Check actual latency and resource use before deciding: no policy is universally best.
Balancing distributes existing capacity. More API servers can help when API processing is the bottleneck; they do not remove a saturated shared database bottleneck.

Headroom is spare capacity. After one backend fails, the survivors need enough capacity for the remaining load. Otherwise redirecting traffic can overload them. Limit or reject excess work visibly instead of assuming redistribution solves it.

A lone balancer is itself a possible failure point. If it fails, clients need a reachable alternate entry path, not just another disconnected balancer box. Use an available managed entry or redundant frontends with working failover, and test that path.

answers.answer: A 200 from the health endpoint only shows that endpoint can answer; it does not establish that purchases can use their required database. The check should reflect capabilities needed for useful new work. Even an improved check has limited coverage, periodic intervals and failure thresholds; the server can fail just after passing, delaying detection. Removing it from eligible backends stops new selections, but requests underway can still fail. Removal neither completes nor undoes nor safely replays those requests. The product all-unhealthy policy also matters because some balancers send to unhealthy targets if all fail their checks.

evidence.quote: A health check periodically probes a backend. Readiness means it can accept useful new work: a process can answer /health while the note handler cannot reach its required database.
Use a check that reflects the capabilities needed to serve notes. Checks have limited coverage, intervals and failure thresholds; a backend can fail just after passing. Detection takes time.
Once detected and removed from eligible backends, it stops receiving new selections. Requests already underway can still fail; removal does not complete, undo or safely replay them.
Check the product's all-unhealthy policy too. Some balancers send traffic to unhealthy targets when every target fails its checks, rather than refusing all traffic.

answers.answer: B cannot read the cart kept only in A memory, and losing A can lose the sole cart copy. Stickiness prefers the same backend and can keep ordinary requests on A, but it can skew load and restrict placement. It neither copies the cart nor guarantees its survival when A fails. Shared session storage lets either backend read it, at the cost of access or coordination work and a shared dependency whose availability also matters.

evidence.quote: Session state is information kept between a user's requests. If the Notes API keeps a user's session only in A's memory, B cannot read it. Losing A can lose the only copy.
Prefers the same backend for that user's requests. It can keep ordinary requests on A, but skew load and restrict placement. It does not copy the session or preserve it when A fails.
Lets either backend read the session. It adds access or coordination work and a shared dependency whose availability matters too.

answers.answer: First stop new assignments to A, then allow already accepted work such as the 20-second request to finish within a bounded drain deadline. Address existing connection lifetimes or stop accepting further HTTP requests too. Shut down after accepted work completes or when the deadline expires. At expiry forced termination may interrupt unfinished requests; their work is not automatically moved to B. Stopping new L4 connections alone leaves a reused existing connection able to carry new HTTP requests. Draining therefore needs to handle the connection and request units involved; even request-aware L7 draining must track accepted work.

evidence.quote: During a deployment, draining stops new assignments to A while allowing in-flight work, meaning requests already underway, to finish within a deadline. Shut A down after completion or when that deadline expires.

Stopping new L4 connections does not stop new HTTP requests on existing connections. A drain must also manage those connection lifetimes or stop accepting further requests. L7 request-aware draining must still track already accepted work.
Give a running note export time to finish, but bound the wait. Forced termination at the deadline may interrupt unfinished requests. Their work is not automatically moved to B.

answers.answer: Because a write may commit even though its response is lost, the timeout does not tell the client whether the purchase committed. A blind retry on B can create a second purchase. Use one stable idempotency key for the logical purchase across every attempt. All backends use a shared durable database record of its key and result. Atomically insert the database-unique key, create the purchase and store the result in one transaction, committing all or none. A repeat then returns the recorded result without another purchase. Separate check-then-write steps can race or leave a crash gap. A new key on each attempt does not identify the repeat, and a key only in A memory cannot reliably protect retry on B. Bound and delay retries because their extra load consumes capacity and can worsen overload; retry policy alone neither protects against duplicates nor guarantees success.

evidence.quote: A saves a new note, but its response is lost. The client cannot tell whether the write committed. A blind retry on B can create a second note.

A stable ID for one logical operation, reused on every attempt. Deduplication means recognizing a repeat. A new key per retry, or a key remembered only in A's memory, cannot reliably protect a retry on B.

All backends use a shared durable database record of the key and result. In one transaction, insert a key that the database allows only once, create the note and record its result; commit all or none. A repeat returns the recorded result without creating another note. Separate check-then-write steps can race or leave a crash gap.
Bound retry attempts and delay them: extra requests consume capacity and can deepen overload. Retry policy does not replace duplicate protection or guarantee success.
